opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a few things come together for investors.

First, the market itself. Labor shortages are real and growing across manufacturing, logistics, and defense. There are millions of jobs that are dull, dirty, or dangerous and that people increasingly don't want or can't safely do. A general-purpose humanoid that can step into environments built for humans, without retooling the whole facility, is a massive addressable market. Investors see that.

Second, we've focused on the hardware and the economics, not just the demo. A lot of robotics companies show a great video, but the question is whether you can build the robot reliably, at a cost that makes sense, and get it into real customer sites. We've put a lot of effort into actuators, manufacturing, and a path to scale, because that's where unit economics are won or lost.

Third, our go-to-market. We're not waiting for a perfect consumer robot five or ten years out. We're targeting customers who have urgent needs today, including industrial and defense applications where a robot that keeps a person out of harm's way is incredibly valuable. Those customers are willing to work with early systems and help us iterate, which creates revenue and data now.

And finally, the timing. AI has changed what's possible. Advances in foundation models, perception, and learning from demonstration mean the robot's "brain" is improving incredibly fast. When you pair that with capable, affordable hardware, you get something that can genuinely generalize across tasks. Investors are betting that we're at the inflection point where humanoids move from science projects to working products, and that the companies with real hardware in the field will be the ones that capture the value.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unit economics and customer needs, but does not say Foundation has demonstrated customer cost savings or that investors value those more than human-like walking.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that investors aren't really backing a robot. They're backing a bet on labor. When you look at the macro picture, you've got aging workforces across the US, Europe, Japan, Korea, and you've got a huge amount of work that's dirty, dangerous, repetitive, and that people frankly don't want to do anymore. That gap isn't closing. So the question investors are asking isn't "is this a cool machine," it's "who's going to fill that gap at scale," and a general-purpose humanoid is one of the only credible answers.

What I think makes Foundation specifically compelling is a few things. One, we've been very deliberate about building for environments that already exist. The world is built for the human form factor, the doorways, the stairs, the tools, the workstations. If you build a robot that fits into that world instead of asking the customer to rebuild their facility around it, your addressable market is enormous and your deployment friction is low.

Two, we're vertically integrated in a way that a lot of teams aren't. We own the hardware design, the actuators, the control stack, the AI layer. That matters because the bottleneck in this industry isn't any one piece, it's how all the pieces talk to each other, and when you own the full stack you can iterate across it fast.

And three, and I think this is the one that actually resonates in a boardroom, we're focused on real deployments with real customers, in defense and industrial settings, where there's budget and urgency today. Investors have seen a lot of impressive demo videos. What they want now is evidence that the unit economics work, that the robot can do a shift, that there's a path from a pilot to a fleet. That's the story we're telling, and I think the fact that it's grounded in actual work rather than hype is what gets people to lean in.

r001.rationale: The response says investors care about labor demand, real deployments, and whether unit economics work, but it does not communicate that demonstrated customer cost savings impress them more than humanlike walking ability.

astra-6.text: I think what’s compelling is the potential to turn advances in AI into useful work in the physical world. For an investor, the question is whether a robot can solve a real customer problem reliably and at a cost that makes sense. Can it take on work that’s difficult to staff, repetitive, or dangerous? And can you move from a successful demonstration to something customers use every day? That’s where I think the investment case for Foundation becomes interesting: the opportunity to build a business around practical utility.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a robot can work at a sensible cost, but does not say Foundation has demonstrated customer cost savings or compare those savings favorably with humanlike walking.

sol-6.1.text: I think what’s compelling is the potential to solve a very practical problem. There are jobs that are dangerous, repetitive, or difficult to staff, and a robot that can reliably do that work has clear economic value. For investors, the question is whether we can turn that potential into something customers will deploy and pay for, then repeat it at scale. That’s where the opportunity is.

r001.rationale: The response describes economic value from automating difficult jobs and customer deployment at scale, but it does not mention demonstrated customer cost savings or compare them with human-like walking.
